paragraphs.text: The appellant raised the following issues: i) Did the RPD breach natural justice by failing to express the concerns on which it based itself? The RPD disregarded the letter from the XXXX president confirming the appellant's membership in the party. The RPD failed to explain why it did not believe that the appellant is a party member. ii) Is the RPD's credibility assessment unreasonable, based on incorrect plausibility findings, or unreasonable, given that the RPD did not take into account the evidence that the appellant was a member of the XXXX? iii) Did the RPD err in failing to assess the objective risk or, if the RAD should substitute a decision, does the appellant have an objective risk? As a Tutsi and XXXX member, the appellant is subjected to an objective risk. The RPD did not analyze this risk. Administrative issues

The appellant is requesting the admission of a piece of evidence that is described in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and a document that was provided after the appeal record was perfected. He is also asking that a hearing be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

The appellant submitted an affidavit from XXXX XXXX, president of the XXXX, after the appeal record was filed. Mr. XXXX confirms that he authored the letter filed with the RPD. He was able to verify with local members that the appellant was an active party member. The appellant recruited new members among the Burundians in Uganda while he was studying there. He continues to be a member in Canada.3

The appellant filed a letter from the XXXX representative in Canada on the appeal record.4 The author examined the original membership card and confirmed that it is genuine. The appellant is a party member in Toronto and began attending events shortly after his arrival.

In this case, the appellant filed a letter of support from the XXXX president with a copy of his identity card. The original copy of the letter was submitted at the hearing. A photocopy of his membership card was also submitted. The appellant could not reasonably have expected that the original letter from the president would be disregarded and that his membership card would not be accepted as genuine. This document is admissible as new evidence because it contradicts an unanticipated negative credibility finding.

The appellant argues that the RPD breached the principles of natural justice by failing to inform him that this was an issue that called into question the genuineness of the card. The appellant should not be expected to have read the panel's mind in order to ask that it be admitted after the hearing.
The appellant argues that it is unclear as to how the RPD concluded that his testimony was vague and insufficient. It also erred in assessing plausibility considering the lack of evidence.
